title: You will tell a strict inequality from a weak one and say what its solution set is.

canonicalUnits.title: Linear inequalities and their solution sets
canonicalUnits.objective: Distinguish strict from weak inequalities and describe what a solution set is.

structuralChecks.note: Automated structural checks passed. These say the lesson is well-formed and truthfully mapped. They say nothing about whether it teaches the objectives.

lessonContent.learningGoal: You will tell a strict inequality from a weak one and say what its solution set is.

vocabulary.meaning: A statement that one quantity is less than or greater than another.
One using < or >, where the two sides are never equal.
One using ≤ or ≥, where equality is allowed.
The set of all values that make the statement true.

explanation: An equation such as x = 3 is satisfied by one number. An inequality such as x > 3 is satisfied by many: 4 works, so does 3.5, so does 1000.
That is the first thing to notice. An inequality usually has no single answer, and asking "what is x?" is the wrong question. The right one is: which values make it true?
Those values together form the solution set. For x > 3 it is values greater than 3, with 3 excluded.
The symbol matters at exactly one point: the boundary. In x > 3 the value 3 does not satisfy the statement, because 3 is not greater than itself. These are the strict inequalities, < and >.
In x ≥ 3 the value 3 does satisfy it, because the symbol allows equality. These are the weak ones, ≤ and ≥, and their solution sets include the boundary.
So the two statements differ by a single number, 3 — and in every other respect agree. Testing the boundary is the way to tell them apart, and it is where mistakes happen.
Checking a candidate is simple: put the value in and see whether the statement is true. For x > 3, the value 2 gives a false statement, 3 gives a false statement, and 4 gives a true one.

steps.text: Put each value into the statement in turn.
2 is greater than 3 is false; 3 is greater than 3 is false.
steps.reasoning: A number is not greater than itself.
So only 4 of the three belongs to the solution set.

workedExamples.prompt: How does the answer change for x ≥ 3?

steps.reasoning: That changes the boundary and nothing else.

steps.text: 3 is greater than or equal to 3 is true.
2 is still outside and 4 is still inside.
steps.reasoning: The two statements differ by exactly one number.

workedExamples.prompt: Why does an inequality not have a single answer?
workedExamples.answer: Because many values satisfy the comparison, so the answer is a set.

steps.text: An equation names a value; an inequality names a comparison.
steps.reasoning: Many values can compare the same way.
There is no largest one to report.

steps.text: So the answer is a set, not a number.
steps.reasoning: That set is what the rest of the chapter finds and draws.

guidedPractice.rationale: They never allow the two sides to be equal.
The weak symbol permits the two sides to be equal.

guidedPractice.answer: The set of all values making the statement true.
guidedPractice.rationale: An inequality is usually satisfied by many values.

independentPractice.rationale: The symbol is strict, so equality does not count.

independentPractice.prompt: Is x > 1 satisfied by more than one value?
Where do a strict and a weak inequality with the same boundary differ?
independentPractice.answer: Only at the boundary value itself.
independentPractice.rationale: Everywhere else the two statements agree.

reasoningApplication.prompt: Why does so much depend on one value at the boundary, when every other number behaves the same in both statements?
reasoningApplication.expectedReasoning: Because the boundary is the only place the two statements can be told apart, which makes it the only place an error shows. Everywhere else a mistake about strict versus weak is invisible — 4 and 1000 satisfy both forms — so a student can carry the confusion a long way without it costing anything, and then meet it at exactly the moment it matters. That is also why the picture of a solution set marks the boundary specially rather than just shading: the shading agrees in both cases, and only the endpoint carries the distinction.

lessonContent.summary: An inequality is usually satisfied by many values, and those values form its solution set. Strict symbols, < and >, exclude the boundary: 3 does not satisfy x > 3. Weak symbols, ≤ and ≥, include it. The two forms differ at the boundary and nowhere else, so testing that value is how to tell them apart.
